turns.user: Can a landlord evict a tenant without giving any notice in India?
turns.answer:
No, a landlord generally cannot evict a tenant without giving notice in India, especially if there is no written contract or local law to the contrary.

According to Section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, if there is no contract or local law or usage stating otherwise, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes is considered a year-to-year lease, which can be terminated by either the landlord or tenant with six months' notice [1]. For any other purpose, a lease of immovable property is considered a month-to-month lease, terminable by either the landlord or tenant with fifteen days' notice [1]. This period of notice begins from the date the notice is received [1]. The notice must be in writing, signed by or on behalf of the person giving it, and can be sent by post, delivered personally to the party or a family member/servant at their residence, or affixed to a conspicuous part of the property if personal delivery is not practical [1]. A notice is not invalid just because the period mentioned in it is shorter than specified, as long as a suit or proceeding is filed after the specified period has expired [1].

General background (not from the retrieved sources):
Tenancy laws in India are complex and can vary significantly depending on the state where the property is located. Many states have their own rent control acts that provide specific procedures and grounds for eviction, often requiring a formal eviction suit to be filed in court after the notice period.

turns.user: My employer has not paid my salary for the last two months. How can I recover it?
turns.answer:
You can recover your unpaid salary by filing a claim with an authority appointed by the government under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 [1]. This authority will hear your claim and can direct your employer to pay the delayed wages [1].

Under Section 3 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, every employer is responsible for paying wages to their employees [5]. "Wages" include all remuneration payable for employment or work done, such as salary, allowances, overtime pay, and any additional remuneration like bonuses [2]. Deductions from wages are generally not allowed unless specifically authorized by or under this Act [4].

The appropriate government can appoint various officers, such as a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation, a Regional Labour Commissioner, an Assistant Labour Commissioner, or a presiding officer of a Labour Court, to hear and decide claims arising from delayed payment of wages [1]. When you file an application, the authority will hear both you and your employer, or give you both an opportunity to be heard [1]. After any necessary inquiry, the authority may direct the employer to pay the delayed wages along with compensation [1]. This compensation can be between one thousand five hundred rupees and three thousand rupees [1]. Even if the delayed wages are paid before the application is resolved, the authority can still direct the payment of compensation, not exceeding two thousand rupees [1]. The aim is to dispose of claims within three months from the date of registration, though this period can be extended [1]. An inquiry under this section is considered a judicial proceeding [1].

If the authority directs payment, and the employer does not comply, the amount can be recovered as if it were a fine [1]. If the authority is a Magistrate, they can recover it as a fine they imposed [1]. If the authority is not a Magistrate, they can apply to a Magistrate for recovery as if it were a fine imposed by that Magistrate [1].

An appeal against an order dismissing an application or directing payment can be made [3]. An employer can appeal if the financial liability imposed exceeds one thousand rupees [3]. An employed person can appeal if the total amount of wages claimed to have been withheld exceeds twenty rupees [3].

General background (not from the retrieved sources):
The Payment of Wages Act, 1936, is a central law in India that regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons. It aims to ensure that wages are paid regularly and without unauthorized deductions.

turns.user: Is an employee entitled to gratuity if they resign before completing 5 years?
turns.answer:
No, an employee is generally not entitled to gratuity if they resign before completing five years of continuous service, unless the termination of employment is due to death or disablement [1].

According to Section 4 of The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, gratuity is payable to an employee upon termination of employment after they have rendered continuous service for not less than five years [1]. This includes termination due to superannuation, retirement, or resignation [1]. However, the requirement of completing five years of continuous service is not necessary if the termination of employment is due to death or disablement [1]. Disablement means an incapacity for the work the employee was capable of performing before the accident or disease [1]. For every completed year of service or part thereof exceeding six months, the employer must pay gratuity at the rate of fifteen days' wages based on the last drawn wages [1].

If there is a dispute regarding the amount of gratuity or who is entitled to it, the employer can deposit the admitted amount with the controlling authority [2]. The employer, employee, or any other person involved in the dispute can apply to the controlling authority to resolve the matter [2]. The controlling authority will conduct an inquiry, give parties a chance to be heard, and then determine the amount payable [2]. If the employer does not pay the gratuity within thirty days from the date it becomes payable, they must pay simple interest [2]. If the gratuity is not paid within the prescribed time, the aggrieved person can apply to the controlling authority, who will issue a certificate to the Collector to recover the amount with compound interest as arrears of land revenue [3]. The controlling authority must give the employer a reasonable opportunity to show cause before issuing such a certificate [3].

General background (not from the retrieved sources):
Gratuity is a lump sum payment made by an employer to an employee as a token of appreciation for their services. It is one of the many retirement benefits offered to employees in India.

turns.user: I bought a defective product online and the company refuses to replace it. What should I do?
turns.answer:
If you bought a defective product online and the company refuses to replace it, you can file a complaint under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. This Act allows a consumer to make a complaint in writing for obtaining relief when goods bought suffer from one or more defects [2].

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
*   A "complainant" can be a consumer, a voluntary consumer association, the Central Government or any State Government, the Central Authority, or one or more consumers with the same interest [2]. In case of a consumer's death, their legal heir or representative can complain, and for a minor, their parent or legal guardian can complain [2].
*   A "complaint" is a written allegation made by a complainant to get relief under the Act [2]. This includes allegations that goods bought or agreed to be bought suffer from one or more defects [2].
*   The Central Authority has an Investigation Wing, headed by a Director-General, to conduct inquiries or investigations under this Act as directed by the Central Authority [1]. The Central Government appoints the Director-General and other officers like Additional Director-General, Director, Joint Director, Deputy Director, and Assistant Director, who have experience in investigation [1]. These officers exercise their powers under the general control and supervision of the Director-General [1]. The Director-General can also delegate powers to these officers for inquiries or investigations [1].
*   The inquiries or investigations made by the Director-General must be submitted to the Central Authority in a specified form, manner, and time [1].
*   The Central Government provides the Central Authority with the necessary officers and employees for its functions [4]. The Central Authority can also engage experts and professionals with special knowledge in areas like consumer rights, law, and product safety to assist it [4].
*   A vacancy or defect in the constitution of the Central Authority, a defect in the appointment of a Chief Commissioner or Commissioner, or any procedural irregularity not affecting the case's merits will not invalidate any act or proceeding of the Central Authority [3].
*   The Central Government also establishes the Central Consumer Protection Council, known as the Central Council, which is an advisory council [5]. The Minister-in-charge of the Department of Consumer Affairs in the Central Government is the Chairperson of this council [5].

General background (not from the retrieved sources):
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, aims to protect the interests of consumers and provides mechanisms for redressal of consumer grievances.
